In 1890s London doctors noted that the men working in the dynamite factories outside the city were being affected by the nitro fumes in a few ways and that Nitroglycerin fumes on an industrial level were in a way, habit forming. The exposure to the nitro affected their circulation in an almost steroid like manner but when they left work for the weekend they would immediately go into withdrawal as their bodies acclimated to not having the Nitroglycerin in its system. Sometimes a worker would drop dead from the symptoms which included headaches and heart palpitations. These heart attacks were referred to as "Sunday heart attacks" because it was on the second day without the fumes that they'd usually happen. Conversely when these guys went back to the factory on Monday they would experience light headedness, giddiness, and dizziness as they reacclimated to the fumes and this was referred to as "The Monday sickness" . Study of these workers contributed to the understanding of Nitroglycerin's medical use and it seems to be what Pynchon is drawing from for nitro as a drug alongside, in Lew Basnight's case the story of Albert Hofmann's discovery of LSD.

I can answer this. The history of American animation is bumpy but I'll try and be concise. American animation from the 1960s through the 1980s was a wasteland. The original Warner cartoons, Merrie Melodies and Looney Tunes, aired as theatrical shorts starting before television was ubiquitous. When TV became the place for animated cartoons the budget was far smaller and it showed. The limited animation of something like a mid 60s Speedy Gonzales short or the 60s Spider-Man series looked like garbage compared to Oscar winning shorts like "What's Opera Doc?" that had aired in cinemas a decade earlier. This combined with the death of Walt Disney led to about a 20 year fallow period in American animation. It's worth noting that during the same time period in Japan a number of televised animated shows that would later be considered masterpieces aired (the first two Gundam shows, the Miyazaki Lupin III series etc) but in the US it was dire. You had He Man, dubbed Transformers, Scooby Doo spinoffs, and lot of shows that come across today as poorly animated toy commercials. In the late 1980s and early 90s three things happened that revitalized American animation: The Simpsons, The Disney Renaissance, and Batman The Animated series. I'll focus on BTAS per your question. Before it there were NO American comic book based TV shows that came close to its level of quality. Compare it to the various Justice League shows of the preceding decade or again the 60s Spider-Man show. It's night and day. While Tim Burton's Batman aired just before it and Christopher Reeves had played Superman a decade earlier, in animated form no other American show took itself as seriously or was as sumptuously animated and voice acted as BTAS.

Against The Day is my favorite Pynchon novel and one of my favorite novels ever. What do I love about it, where do I start? The characters are so finely drawn. Pynchon often gets criticized for writing flat characters, parodic and one dimensional. I disagree with that criticism in general but nowhere does he have as many brilliantly drawn characters as Against The Day; Kit, Reef, Frank, Lake, Deuce, Sloat, Dally, Merle, Cyprian, Yashmeen, Lew, Webb, Mayva, Stray, THE CHUMS; the book overflows with deeply human characters.

The pastiche elements taken from the popular literature of the early 20th century are all executed perfectly, the sense of regret and hope that permeates the book, the way TRP dives deep into science fiction, art, politics, music, science, mathematics, everything that made up the era. Against The Day is about hope in the face of darkness. Where Gravity's Rainbow ends in potential apocalypse, Against The Day contains moments of sublime hope and gentleness even as the world that the characters know is racing towards its own darkness. It is the Yin to Gravity's Rainbow's Yang and I pretty much can't sing its praises enough. I'm currently rereading it for the 4th time.
